name: Ganelon
summary: The largest crewed utility spaceplane in the fleet — a reusable TSTO lifting-body that carries 50 t to LEO and lands under its own control.
description: The LX-23 Ganelon is KnightShip’s heavy orbital flagship: the largest crewed utility spaceplane in the fleet. It is a two-stage-to-orbit lifting-body spaceplane, launched on three TX-04 Pauldrons, that carries up to 50 t to low Earth orbit and lands under its own control. All figures are preliminary concept-phase estimates; none has yet been through CFD or trajectory simulation.

specs.range: LEO (to the MX-79 node) and return; beyond-LEO via carried transfer vehicle

deltaV.note: Stage 1 = boosters (pad→staging). Stage 2 = LX-23 own tanks (staging→orbit). ~310 m/s working after ~130 m/s deorbit.

specs.landing: belly-flop → lifting-body glide → dead-stick ~89 m/s (~321 km/h)

components.name: Lifting-body hull
components.what: Near-wingless; the hull itself generates lift and IS the propellant tank
components.detail: Flat shielded underside is the re-entry heat-shield plane; smooth domed top; widens 2 m nose → 15 m tail.

components.name: Main engines
components.detail: Burn LCH4/LOX; the tail houses engines and provides aft planform area for lift.

components.name: Boiloff-fed dual-mode thrusters
components.what: One set does RCS, OMS, and propulsive landing
components.detail: Rotate on a swivel; fed warm gas (RCS) or liquid+ignite (OMS aimed along velocity / Landing aimed down). Removes dedicated OMS.

components.name: Boiloff canisters
components.detail: Recapture gas that would be vented; merge attitude control with zero-boiloff management.

components.name: X-fins
components.what: Aft control surfaces (4, in an X)
components.detail: Thin control fins, not large wings.

components.name: Module bays
components.detail: ~300 m3 cargo; fits landers, GEO tugs, 15 m station modules, satellites to ~14 m.

capabilities.name: Cargo hauler
capabilities.detail: ~50 t payload in a ~300 m3 bay; carries dense/wide cargo nothing smaller in the fleet can.

capabilities.name: Tanker
capabilities.detail: Hull mostly tank → ~985 t propellant to orbit, delivering ~50 t methalox to the MX-79 node per trip.

capabilities.name: Carrier
capabilities.detail: Bay fits a lander, a GEO transfer vehicle, large station modules (15 m wide), or satellites to ~14 m.

capabilities.name: Station
capabilities.detail: Gross 1,713 m3 vs ISS habitable ~915 m3 — outfitted with modules it rivals a small station, then lands. Its distinctive identity: station-class volume that returns to Earth and reflies.

capabilities.name: Pseudo deep-space (fully fuelled)
capabilities.detail: Refuelled in orbit, full-tank vacuum Δv ~7,780 m/s (50 t) / ~9,740 m/s empty — enough to throw 50 t to Mars orbit and even return. Lacks the long-duration life support of a true LX-24; the propulsion closes, the habitability does not.

modules.name: GEO transfer vehicle
modules.purpose: Released in LEO, self-flies to GEO (LX-23 does not fly to GEO itself)

modules.name: Lander
modules.purpose: Carried to LEO/handed off for surface missions

modules.name: Station modules
modules.purpose: Up to 15 m wide; build an orbital outpost

calculations.title: Hull volume (D-section integration)
calculations.method: Integrate D-section cross-sections along 45 m at 15 m max width; area = (π/4)·W·H per station, trapezoidal along length.
calculations.result: Gross ~1,713 m3; −12% structural void → usable ~1,508 m3; −cargo 300 −crew 40 −systems 100 → tank ~1,068 m3 → ~886 t methalox at 830 kg/m3.
calculations.note: Widening 14→15 m nearly doubled internal volume vs the old 8 m body and took the vehicle from volume-starved to closing.

calculations.title: Dry mass build-up (bottom-up)
calculations.method: Sum itemized subsystems, then +15% growth margin.
calculations.result: structure 27 + TPS 8 + propulsion 9 + gear 1.5 + hab 3.4 + avionics/power/shield 5.3 = ~53 t; +15% ≈ ~60 t.
calculations.note: Payload trades ~1:1 with dry mass. 50 t holds if dry ≤ ~60 t.

calculations.title: Per-stage Δv (from real TX-04 masses)
calculations.method: Asparagus with crossfeed: LX-23 mains draw from booster tanks so LX-23 separates full. Stage 1 MR from 3×TX-04 pushing the stack; Stage 2 MR from LX-23 full tank.
calculations.result: Stage 1 ~3,660 m/s (Isp 330), Stage 2 ~7,780 m/s (Isp 360). Total ~11,440 m/s vs ~11,000 needed → ~440 m/s reserve at 50 t.
calculations.note: ~310 m/s working after ~130 m/s deorbit — enough for rendezvous, docking, phasing, trims, return unaided.

calculations.title: Hydrolox rejection (volume)
calculations.method: Compare tank volume to hold equal impulse.
calculations.result: Hydrolox needs ~1,970 m3 vs ~1,068 m3 available — ~1.8× too much (LH2 bulk ~360 vs methalox ~830 kg/m3).
calculations.note: LX-23 is volume-limited, so the denser propellant wins despite lower Isp.

blueprint.frame: Length 45 m; max width 15 m at the tail tapering to ~2 m at the nose; peak height 4.5 m. Flat bottom, domed top (D-section).
blueprint.stations: Bridge/crew/hab forward; two module bays ~stations 8–24 m; aft control X-fins; forward fore-fin pair; engines at the broad 15 m tail.

sections.heading: Mission
sections.body: The LX-23 delivers up to 50 t of payload, or two large modules, to low Earth orbit and returns. It reaches orbit under its own power with a modest maneuvering reserve (~440 m/s) and does its orbital work unaided. Refuelling at the MX-79 node is optional — used only to extend on-orbit Δv or stage a mission beyond LEO, not to reach orbit. Missions beyond LEO ride as a carried payload-vehicle released from the bay.

sections.heading: Launch architecture — asparagus
sections.body: Launches on three TX-04 Pauldrons in asparagus staging. Liftoff: all three Pauldrons and the LX-23 mains fire together, all drawing from the outer pair first so the center stays full. Outer pair drains and drops; remaining engines draw from the center; center drains and drops; the LX-23 continues to orbit on its own full tanks. Asparagus sheds each dead tank the instant it empties — the most mass-efficient staging known. The TX-04s are the methalox variant so they crossfeed the LX-23 mains and each other.

sections.heading: Higher orbits — GEO by carried vehicle
sections.body: The LX-23 does not fly itself to GEO. A LEO-to-GEO round trip on one tank would need ~98% propellant fraction — impossible. Instead GEO and beyond are payload: the LX-23 carries a dedicated transfer vehicle in its bay, reaches LEO, and releases it; the transfer vehicle makes the climb itself, refuelable at the node and reusable.

sections.heading: Re-entry & landing
sections.body: Re-enters belly-first at high angle of attack, presenting the flat shielded underside, then transitions to a lifting-body glide and lands dead-stick at ~89 m/s. The belly-flop-to-glide transition is the highest-risk open item: the center of pressure moves through the pitch-down, and stability depends on where the center of mass sits relative to that moving CoP. A coupled trajectory-and-attitude simulation is required to confirm it.

changelog.why: Bottom-up dry mass came in at ~61 t (later trimmed to 60); 50 t gives a real ~440 m/s on-orbit reserve instead of near-zero.
Volume recompute showed 14 m held only ~736 t; 15 m holds ~886 t and closes with reserve.
Three fleet-common TX-04s (methalox) reach 50 t via asparagus; no bespoke heavy core needed. Fleet flies on one booster.
120 m3 was station-generous (30 m3/person); a basic 4-person hab is ~40 m3. Freed volume went to tank.

decisions.why: Volume — hydrolox needs ~1.8× the tank (1,970 vs 1,068 m3). LX-23 is volume-limited.
One booster across the whole fleet (EX=1, VX=2, LX=3) is worth more than the ~20 t extra payload a bespoke core would add.
The hull generates lift AND is the tank; deleting wings drops dry mass and the lift-shape holds propellant instead of being dead mass.
55 t closed with near-zero reserve; 50 t leaves ~440 m/s for real orbital maneuvering and unaided return.

openItems: Belly-flop-to-glide transition: CoP travel vs CoG — needs coupled trajectory/attitude sim (highest-risk item).
Lifting-body L/D across flight regimes — needs CFD.
Detailed tank-vs-bay volume split (sets true tank fraction of the 1,068 m3).
Thruster GOX materials, canister pressure on long coasts, ullage settling before in-orbit liquid burns, engine-out authority in ignited landing.
Shared RCS/OMS/landing duty cycle counted against thruster reuse life.
